claims.text: The Pulumi support index page links to a page at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ ("Provider support policy"), which must exist in the docs.
The Pulumi provider support policy page (/docs/support/provider-support-policy/) explains how long Pulumi maintains each provider major version.
Pulumi provides long-term security updates for some providers (and not others); the provider support policy page identifies which providers get long-term security updates.

Pulumi does not automatically roll back changes made during an update if an error or failure occurs; it completes any pending operations currently in progress, then exits and reports the error or failure.

To perform a manual rollback after a failed Pulumi deployment, reverting the code and configuration changes of the failed deployment and running `pulumi up` returns the infrastructure to its previous state.

Pulumi does not automatically query the cloud provider's live state before running `pulumi up` or `pulumi preview`; it compares the desired state declared in the program against the last recorded state to determine what changes to make.

Pulumi's not refreshing state automatically before every update is an intentional design decision, because refreshing requires a round-trip to the cloud provider for every resource in a stack, adding significant latency for large stacks.
Pulumi's design philosophy is that the program is the source of truth for desired state, and changes made outside of Pulumi are treated as drift that the user decides explicitly how to handle.
Running `pulumi refresh` synchronizes Pulumi's recorded state with the actual state of the cloud resources.
`pulumi up --refresh` refreshes state and applies the desired state in a single step.
Pulumi Cloud provides built-in drift detection for automated drift detection and remediation on a schedule (Pulumi Deployments drift detection).
The page /docs/deployments/concepts/drift/ exists and documents Pulumi Cloud drift detection.
The page /docs/iac/concepts/state-and-backends/ has a 'Refreshing state' section (#refreshing-state) that explains refresh behavior in detail.
In Pulumi, a resource's logical name is how the resource is known to Pulumi and is part of the auto-assigned resource URN, while the physical name is how the resource is known to the cloud provider.
A Pulumi resource's logical name only needs to be unique within a stack, while the physical name typically needs to be unique within a certain scope (sometimes even globally).

Pulumi automatically creates each resource's physical name by combining the logical name with a random suffix appended afterwards, so that many logical resources and stacks can be stood up side-by-side without conflicts.
Pulumi's auto-naming with random suffixes lets Pulumi replace resources with less downtime by creating the replacement before deleting the old resource.
An auto-named Pulumi resource's physical name will typically look like `my-bucket-d7c2fa0` instead of `my-bucket` (random hex suffix).

Auto-naming can be disabled on a per-resource basis in Pulumi, which allows precise physical names without random suffixes but loses the benefits of side-by-side stack deployment and create-before-delete replacement.
The page /docs/iac/concepts/resources/names/ has an '#autonaming' section describing auto-naming.
Pulumi project or stack configuration can be used to customize or disable auto-naming globally, per provider, or per resource type.
The page /docs/iac/concepts/resources/names/ has an '#autonaming-configuration' section titled 'Auto-naming Configuration'.
Pulumi provides primitives so users can enforce that secrets are stored securely in the CLI, state file, and Pulumi Cloud.
During a Pulumi update, secrets are decrypted in memory and visible to the Pulumi program.
The page /docs/iac/concepts/secrets/ has a '#secrets' section.
Passing `--secret` to `pulumi config set` causes the configuration value to be encrypted so it can be safely persisted in `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml`.
For every stack, Pulumi Cloud manages a unique encryption key used to encrypt secrets for that stack, and this is configurable to use a custom secrets provider.
Because a different encryption key is used per stack, encrypting the same value across two different stacks results in different encrypted strings in the `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml` files.
An encrypted Pulumi config value cannot be copied from one stack config file to another with a text editor; `pulumi config set` must be used instead.

When running a Pulumi preview, update, or destroy, Pulumi decrypts secret config data; it is plain text during execution and any part of the Pulumi program may access it using the Pulumi config object.
Pulumi does not use the Terraform engine in any way.
Some Pulumi providers use the open-source Terraform schemas to know what resources and parameters are available and to determine return and response attributes.
Pulumi native providers are mapped directly to the cloud provider APIs and do not use Terraform schemas.
The link https://www.terraform.io/docs/extend/schemas/index.html and the blog post /blog/pulumiup-native-providers/ exist and support the Terraform schema / native provider statements.
Pulumi is a declarative tool that uses imperative languages to define the end state; the language is used for authoring the program and not for talking to the cloud provider API.
Pulumi uses strongly typed languages that support IntelliSense and the Language Server Protocol, so when defining Pulumi programs users rarely need to leave their IDE.
Experimental Pulumi features are always opt-in, enabled explicitly with a flag, command, or environment variable (such as `PULUMI_EXPERIMENTAL=true`).
`PULUMI_EXPERIMENTAL=true` is an environment variable that enables experimental Pulumi functionality.
Pulumi experimental features are not necessarily supported and can change or be removed at any time without a deprecation cycle.
When an experimental feature proves valuable, Pulumi invests in stabilizing it and promoting it to general availability.
Pulumi's provider version support policy is to focus on actively supporting the latest released major version of the providers Pulumi maintains.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi also ships security updates for the previous major version for up to a year, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
The provider support policy page (/docs/support/provider-support-policy/) lists the covered providers and what a long-term support release contains.
Older major versions of Pulumi-maintained providers (beyond the latest major and, for widely used providers, the previous major's security-update window) receive no patches at all.
The Pulumi Registry (/registry/) lists the current version for all providers maintained by Pulumi.

Major provider versions typically include significant changes such as deprecations, new resources and new functionality, which may require additional migration steps; a major release is a signal to begin planning a provider version update.
Minor provider versions typically include new resources and features, performance improvements, and bug fixes without introducing breaking changes.
Pulumi recommends, at least quarterly, considering updating to the latest minor version on the current major provider version and minimally reviewing provider release notes.
The release notes for each Pulumi provider release summarize the new capabilities or fixes.
Using the tilde operator in npm (e.g., `~1.2.3`) allows patch updates on the current minor version.
Patch versions of Pulumi providers are primarily for bug fixes and security updates and are designed to be fully backward compatible.
Pulumi recommends always allowing patch updates on the current minor version of a provider.
Pulumi advises never being two major provider versions behind, because jumping a major version is inadvisable due to potential breaking changes across major versions.

Each major version of a Pulumi provider includes migration logic to smooth the upgrade from the immediately previous major version, but these migrations do not always work across multiple major versions.
Being two or more major provider versions behind can accumulate many changes and may require a multi-step upgrade.
The page /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ exists (Provider support policy).
The pages /docs/support/faq/secrets-config/ (Pulumi ESC FAQ), /docs/support/faq/pulumi-cloud/ (Pulumi Cloud FAQ), and /docs/support/faq/policies/ (Pulumi Policies FAQ) exist.
Pulumi actively maintains the latest released major version of every provider it publishes.

For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi ships security updates for the previous major version (N−1) for up to 12 months, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first (the 12 months being measured from N's release, per the summary table).
The providers that receive long-term support are described as 'widely used providers'.

The providers that currently receive long-term support (LTS) updates on eligible older versions are: AWS, Azure Classic, Azure Native, Azure AD, Command, Docker Build, GCP, Kubernetes, TLS, and Vault.

The Pulumi Registry has package pages at /registry/packages/aws/, /registry/packages/azure/ (Azure Classic), /registry/packages/azure-native/, /registry/packages/azuread/, /registry/packages/command/, /registry/packages/docker-build/, /registry/packages/gcp/, /registry/packages/kubernetes/, /registry/packages/tls/, and /registry/packages/vault/, matching the providers named in the LTS list.
Pulumi provider LTS branch releases ship High/Critical CVE security patches, including fixes for CVEs affecting the provider's code or its direct dependencies.
Pulumi provider LTS branch releases include fixes for broken internal infrastructure on the LTS branch when needed to ship the CVE security patches.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain new upstream API versions.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain new resources or new resource properties.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain performance improvements.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain non-security bug fixes.
A Pulumi provider LTS release does not contain compatibility with newer versions of language runtimes.
Pulumi providers on the LTS branch remain compatible with the version of the Pulumi engine they were frozen at, unless security fixes prompt otherwise.
Under Pulumi's provider support policy, exactly one long-term support major version exists per covered provider at any time.
When a new major version N+1 of a covered provider ships, it becomes the new N and the old N becomes the new LTS major.
When N+1 ships, the previous LTS major version reaches end of life on the same day, regardless of how much of its 12-month window remained.
Within the long-term support major version of a covered provider, only the latest minor version receives patches; earlier minor versions are frozen.
Pulumi provider LTS releases are available through the same standard package registries as current-major releases, but are tagged differently.
Customers who pin to a specific major version of a covered provider automatically receive patch releases as they ship; pinning to a specific major version is the recommended approach.
At any time, exactly one major version of a covered provider is the LTS version, and older majors (N−2 and earlier) receive no patches.
N is the latest released major version: if v3 is the newest release, then v3 is N, v2 is N−1 (LTS), and v1 and earlier are end of life.

The current major version (N) of a Pulumi provider is supported until N+1 ships, and ships new features, new resources, bug fixes, security patches, dependency upgrades, and new upstream API versions.
The long-term support version (N−1) of a covered Pulumi provider ships security updates in the provider's code or its direct dependencies.
End-of-life provider versions (N−2 and older) are not supported and will not receive updates.

The Pulumi support FAQ at /docs/support/faq/infrastructure/ has a section with anchor 'what-are-the-best-practices-for-maintaining-provider-versions' on best practices for maintaining provider versions.
The Pulumi Registry exists at /registry/.
A 'Getting support' page exists at /docs/support/getting-support/.
